paragraphs.text: This is [Gong Ting](gong-ting:definition), the grade of loose [ripe pu’er](shou:definition) sorted out for its small leaf and high share of buds, one step above special grade in the market. The dry leaf is tight and fine, with [golden down on the buds](gong-ting:appearance) and no stray stems. So little of a batch qualifies that the grade stays scarce. Here the leaf has been shaped into a ball.

The leaf comes from [Menghai County](menghai-county:county-and-factory) in Yunnan. It was fermented in a [damp pile](shou:wet-piling), where microbes warm the leaf from within. The pile is covered to hold that heat and turned about once a week to let air in. That pile is why the tea is ready to drink now rather than after years of waiting. In this county, the factory's own way of piling had settled [by 1975](shou:piling-1973) into the ripe pu’er still made today.

brewing.text: From a cake, brick or tuo, ease a piece off along the edge with a pick rather than snapping it. Whole leaves give up their flavour steadily; broken ones release it all at once and cloud the cup. Ripe pu’er takes boiling water: fermented, tightly packed leaf needs full heat to open, and it does not scald the way green tea can. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and one quick rinse, which wakes the leaf and carries off dust and any pile smell. Then short steeps that lengthen as the leaf opens, so the cup stays clear rather than heavy; it gives eight or more good cups.

notice.text: A smooth, sweet cup with earthy or woody notes. A young ripe tea can carry a faint smell of the pile, which fades with airing or in the first steeps.
